summary:
MARNAV — High-Level Summary

Exploring Mars presents significant challenges, including hazardous terrain, extreme environmental conditions, and limited astronaut life-support resources. Safe exploration requires reliable navigation, scientific information, and continuous astronaut monitoring.

MARNAV is an intelligent Mars navigation and astronaut safety platform designed to integrate these capabilities into one interactive system.

The platform aims to combine seven scientific data layers—optical, thermal, spectral, topographic, geophysical, atmospheric, and chemical—with intelligent route planning that compares the shortest and safest paths. It also aims to monitor essential astronaut parameters, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, remaining oxygen supply, and spacesuit battery levels.

Our current prototype features an interactive 3D map of Jezero Crater's Three Forks region, built using real NASA/USGS HiRISE elevation data, with elevation inspection and slope visualization. Additional scientific layers, route optimization, and astronaut monitoring are under development.

MARNAV aims to improve astronaut safety, situational awareness, and mission efficiency during future Mars exploration.
details:
MARNAV (Intelligent Mars Navigation & Astronaut Safety System) is a browser-based Mars exploration and mission-support platform developed by Team Apollo11 for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project combines interactive 3D Mars mapping, scientific data visualization, terrain-based route planning, simulated rover operations, and astronaut safety monitoring. Built using React, Vite, JavaScript, Three.js, and React Three Fiber, MARNAV features an interactive Mars globe, mission markers, an astronaut helmet-style dashboard, and dedicated modules for scientific exploration, rover simulation, and astronaut resources. The NASA Science & Routes module incorporates planetary datasets obtained from NASA and USGS, including HiRISE-derived elevation data from the Three Forks region of Jezero Crater. Using GDAL and terrain analysis techniques, the project processes elevation and slope information to support scientific visualization and the development of shortest-distance and terrain-aware safer route calculations. The platform also explores multiple scientific data categories, including optical, thermal, spectral, topographic, geophysical, atmospheric, and chemical information, with radiation-related information available as a conceptual category.

MARNAV also includes simulated astronaut and spacesuit monitoring interfaces designed to display essential information such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, oxygen supply, battery levels, environmental conditions, and mission resources. Its objective is to improve situational awareness and support safer, more efficient Mars exploration by bringing navigation, scientific information, and astronaut safety tools into one accessible environment. The current prototype includes a functional 3D Mars interface, mission dashboard, module launchers, and developed terrain-analysis and route-planning components, although some modules operate as separate local applications and require further integration and testing. A successful local production build has been completed, while public deployment, route validation, and full system integration remain ongoing. Scientific measurements are distinguished from simulated readings and conceptual visualizations, and calculated routes are not NASA-certified. Future development will focus on completing public deployment, validating navigation algorithms, integrating additional scientific datasets, improving astronaut safety alerts, and connecting the platform with real monitoring systems. MARNAV demonstrates how NASA planetary data and modern web technologies can contribute to future human exploration of Mars.
